questions.q: From a single pixel of a monocular camera you can recover:
questions.explain: The distance along the ray is unknown; you need height above a plane, stereo, the object's size or a rangefinder.

questions.q: A 1280 px camera with a 90° horizontal field of view. f_x in pixels:
The “undistort” function for a measured pixel is usually computed:
options: By plugging into the same formula
It isn't needed for wide angles
questions.explain: The model describes how an ideal point is distorted; the inverse problem is solved iteratively (undistortPoints).

questions.q: A calibration reprojection RMS of 1.8 px most likely means:
questions.explain: Motion blur, too few tilted views, a board that isn't flat, or stabilization turned on. Good is < 0.5 px, acceptable up to 1 px.

questions.q: Nadir camera, altitude 100 m, 1° roll error. The shift on the ground of the point below the vehicle:
The main source of frame georeferencing error during maneuvers:
options: Frame and attitude out of sync
questions.explain: At 100°/s a 50 ms offset is 5° of attitude, which is meters on the ground.

questions.q: As distance increases, a stereo camera's depth error grows:
options: As the square of the distance

questions.q: If the camera is on a gimbal, the pixel → ground chain uses:
questions.explain: GIMBAL_DEVICE_ATTITUDE_STATUS: the camera is stabilized, so its orientation is the gimbal's orientation.

questions.q: All ground points are off by tens of meters, more so when the vehicle tilts. The matrix from the calibration file for a 1280×720 frame:
options: The principal point (c_x, c_y) = (0, 0) instead of ~(640, 360): the calibration is corrupted or the wrong one was loaded
A focal length of 812 px is too large for 1280 px: it should be about 400 px with any lens
The matrix has no distortion coefficients, and their absence shifts every point by exactly half a frame
f_x and f_y differ by 0.5 px, which is enough for an error of tens of meters
questions.explain: Without the principal point every ray is off by half a frame; the error grows with altitude and tilt.
